findings.title: Credential lifetime and handling
findings.requirement: Issue short-lived credentials from a trusted issuer or managed identity service. For API calls, use expiring access tokens with a specific destination audience, identifying the agent and any explicitly delegated user or system authority, rather than static API keys or personal access tokens. A secrets vault stores backing secrets; it does not itself make a static key into an expiring access token. Keep long-lived secrets out of prompts, images, and checked-in config. Where supported, bind tokens to their holder (mTLS, DPoP, or workload proof tokens). Don't use fixed API keys when short-lived or federated credentials are available. If only static keys are supported, isolate them at the enforcement layer, limit their permissions, and record the lifetime and revocation gap. Show expiry and rotation, including allowed overlap, and explain the chosen lifetime.

No way to cut off the agent's access without cutting off the user
Secrets showing up in tool output, responses, or normal logs
Container image not pinned by digest or signature-checked

findings.title: Destructive-action interception
findings.requirement: List the high-impact operations. These include deletes, destructive database updates, force-pushes, tearing down infrastructure, payment changes, and sending anything outside. Block them by default in the execution path. Allow one only when a reviewer or system with higher authority approves that specific action. When the action runs, authorize its operation, target, and arguments, and block it if they aren't allowed. A list of blocked words or command names is not enough. Test other tools and raw API or shell paths that could do the same thing. Treat deleting audit records, or changing how long they are kept, as high-impact too. That includes asking a more powerful tool or peer to do it. Some agents can do all three of these in one context: read untrusted input, reach sensitive data or systems, and change things or talk to the outside. For those agents, treat every consequential action as high-impact. The exception is a design that stops untrusted content from picking the tool, destination, or arguments. Examples are plan-then-execute, a two-model pattern, or capability tracking such as CaMeL. Record which of the three each agent type has.

not_covered.problem: Denied actions not recorded in the audit trail
Approvals that can be replayed, reused in parallel, or used after expiry
Outside effects left unreconciled after the agent is stopped
A chain of individually allowed actions that adds up to data theft
Tool output not labelled or kept apart from trusted instructions

findings.title: Minimal, isolated runtime
findings.requirement: Remove shells, downloaders, package managers, mounts, and privileges the agent doesn't need. As a container baseline, meet the Kubernetes Pod Security Standards "restricted" profile or the same controls elsewhere. That means non-root, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped, and a seccomp profile set. findings.title: Retrieval-corpus integrity

Its index stores those documents, or smaller passages called chunks, in a search engine or vector database. Limit which identities and sources can add or change content there. findings.title: Complete release manifest
findings.requirement: Write a release manifest: a list of everything that makes up this release. Include the container, harness, system prompt, rules files, model, built-in tools, MCP servers, permission scopes, memory and retrieval settings, identity bindings, network rules, and execution budgets. Include security-policy versions, MCP protocol and extension versions, approved tool-publication config, issuer/audience bindings, and cache/task isolation settings. Add a separate model record for every model: the main agent model, sub-agent models, and helper models such as embedding models and rerankers. For each, record the provider, model ID, exact version or checkpoint, and any adapter or fine-tune version. For training or fine-tuning you run yourself, also record the training job ID, base-model version, training code and config version, dataset version, and the digest of the output. findings.title: Enforced gateway boundary
findings.requirement: Send MCP calls through a gateway or equivalent enforcement layer the agent cannot bypass. Choose controls for internal HTTP servers, public third-party services, and local stdio servers; private networking and mTLS are one internal deployment pattern, not universal MCP requirements. Authenticate each caller, preserve agent and delegated-subject identity, and authorize each action's tool, operation, resource, tenant, and arguments. Apply the same policy to direct calls, dynamic tools, CLI/code mode, and wrappers. Validate calls and responses, enforce rate limits, and log every decision. For HTTP OAuth, validate access tokens for the gateway's own audience, issuer, expiry, and scopes; obtain separately authorized backend credentials through a trusted issuer or supported exchange. Never accept a token for another resource or relay it unchanged as a substitute for backend authorization. Keep backend secrets and tokens away from agent-controlled execution paths. Restrict local process launch, files, environment, credentials, and network in the host or sandbox. Under MCP 2026-07-28, reject metadata-header/body mismatches before routing or policy relies on them. Isolate private caches by verified authorization context, tenant, resource, and policy version; share only data explicitly approved as public. Authorize explicit task/state handles on every operation; neither a connection nor self-reported metadata establishes identity. Where the gateway is an OAuth client, validate authorization-server issuer responses and protect discovery URLs against SSRF. Record protocol and extension versions and test each enabled extension's boundary, including task access/cancellation and MCP Apps sandbox, CSP, bridge messages, and UI-initiated tool authorization. Test bypass, cross-tenant access, malformed traffic, and required-check outages. Required checks fail closed.

findings.requirement: Give sub-agents only the powers approved for their task. Preserve the verified original subject and current actor through each handoff and enforce their task, tenant, resource, and audience limits where the action runs. findings.title: Protect shared evidence
findings.requirement: Set rules for how long audit records are kept, who can see them, what is redacted, how their integrity is checked, and how they are exported and restored. Test pulling up a past run, and test that missing records or a broken pipeline get noticed. Keep records long enough for investigations and for the law. For example, the EU AI Act requires providers and deployers of high-risk systems to keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (Articles 19 and 26). High-impact actions must fail closed when required audit capture isn't working.
